2. Thy suit was contested by defendant No.1 by filing a written statement admitting that he was the owner of the suit property with possession in the same and that he executed an agreement for sale of the suit property to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 12,00,000.00 out of which he received taka one lac as earnest money on the day of execution of the agreement dated 30-7-79. The case of the defendant is that, he had been a reputed businessman of Dhaka and decided to sell the, suit property in order to raise fund, for enlarging his business and, with this end in view, he entered into a written agreement with the plaintiff to sell the suit property, the consideration being fixed at Taka 12,00,000.00 and the agreement was executed on 30-7-79 when taka one lac was paid as earnest money and it was decided to complete the sale transaction on or before 31st December, 1979, but the defendant having suffered a stroke on 2-11-79 was taken to Mitford Hospital for treatment and was subsequently shifted to PG Hospital, Dhaka, where he received treatment from 30-11-79 to 11-12-1979 and was under treatment of Professor Rashiduddin Ahmed, Neuro Surgeon. The defendant also received treatment in New Delhi under Professor Tandon, Neuron Surgeon, to whom he was referred by Professor Rashiduddin Ahmed, It is further stated that defendant did not recover from his illness and also received treatment in Pakistan under Dr. Jumma, Neuro Surgeon, and Professor Abdur Rob. In the meantime the plaintiff persuaded, Mrs Nasrin Sultana, wife of defendant No.1, to receive taka five lac and she handed over possession of the suit property without permission of her husband; It is further stated in the written statement that the result of the stroke was loss of speech and consciousness, impairment of power to express himself by speech or writing, which is an effect of brain damage, and now the defendant has to move with the help of his wife, Nasrin Sultana, and his business partner, Syed Masud Ali, who look after his business, because he is not physically or mentally capable of managing his business independently, without help from others and has been advised by his doctor to curtail his business activities and reside in a peaceful area to avoid tension. In May/June, 1981, defendant No. 1 personally met the plaintiff along with Syed Masud Ali and requested him to take back taka one lac paid to him and Taka five lac paid to his wife along with reasonable compensation because of change of situation in the life of the defendant. Though plaintiff agreed to consider the matter, unfortunately, he filed the suit against the defendant. It is further averred in the written statement that the Government, a necessary party in the suit for specific performance of contract, was not made a party within the period of limitation and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed because of the bar of limitation. The other point is that, specific performance of contract being an equitable relief should be refused in this case because of hardship the contract would cause to the defendant, who, because of the present state of his health, is not in a position to enlarge his business for which the contract was entered into. 

 4. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Advocate for defendant No. 1 appellant, has submitted that the Court below erred in law in not holding that the suit was not properly constituted because the Government, though a necessary party, was not impleaded at the time of institution of the suit, and at a later stage when the government was added as a party (Pro-defendant No. 2), the suit became barred by limitation. Mr. MI Farooqui further submits that specific performance of contract is an equitable relief, and though it may be lawful to grant it, the Court may refuse to grant this relief in a proper case. The Court below should have considered the hardship of the defendant from his illness that occurred soon after the contract and its effect on his speech and free movement of his body and, in that view of the matter, the trial Court committed an error of law in not refusing the equitable relief of specific performance of contract Mr. Farooqui has, in this connection, referred to the decision in the case of Md Latifur Rahman vs Golam Ahmed Shah, 39 DLR (AD) 242, where specific performance was refused because of hardship it would have caused to the defendant and solatitium was granted to the plaintiff. 

 5. Mr. Nurullah, learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent, has submitted that the suit is within time because the cause of action arose on 8-2-81 on refusal of the defendant to plaintiffs request for execution and registration of the sale deed and the suit was filed on 6-7-81. He submits that the plaintiff filed an application before the trial Court on 31-1-84 for adding the government as a pro-forma defendant in the suit and this application being in time, the suit cannot come within the mischief of limitation. He submits that the application dated 31-1-84 was allowed by the trial Court on 29-3-84 and filing of the application within the period of limitation saved the suit from the mischief of limitation. Mr. Nurullah further submits that the trial Court considered all aspects of the matter for decreeing the suit, because the question of hardship must be judged on the date of the contract and not in the light of the subsequent events and that physical disability of the defendant, if any, which was subsequent to the contract, cannot be argued as a ground of hardship to defeat the suit for specific performance of contract. In support of his contention Mr.Nurullah has referred to the decision in the case of Sankara Lings vs Ratnaswami, AIR 1952 Madras 389 and Qazi Din Mohammad vs Al-Haj Arzan Ali and another, 47 DLR (AD) 48. Nurullah submits that the case of Latifur Rahman and others vs Golam Ahmed Shah 39 DLR (AD) 242, is distinguishable from the facts of the present case and that the ground for solatitium does not apply to the facts and circumstances of the present case. 

 6. It has been strenuously argued by Mr. Farooqui that the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is a necessary party in the suit for specific performance of contract and that the government having not being impleaded in time, the suit was barred by limitation and liable to be dismissed as such. 

 9. Mr Farooqui has further referred to the case of Sobharadri vs Parthasarathi reported in AIR 1932 Madras 583 where a suit was filed for recovery of compensation for fraudulent representation of the defendant at the time of the contract. The plaintiffs’ case is that the defendants sold to the plaintiff and his brother by a conveyance dated 17th February, 1917, certain villages including Penjendra, the suit village. The price of the village in question was fixed at 29 times the net income. The plaintiff claims that subsequently in a partition between him and his brother, that suit villages fell to his share (share of the plaintiff). The case of action in the suit arose on 1-4-1919 when the fraud was discovered and the suit was filed on 14th February, 1920. The plaintiff filed an application on 19th July, 1923, for adding his brother as pro-forma defendant. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court on the ground that the plaintiff is not competent to maintain the action in the absence of his brother, who was necessary party, and that when, on this defect having been pointed out, he applied for his brother being impleaded, the suit was barred by limitation. The appeal was dismissed by the Division Bench of Madras High Court on the ground when necessary parties were not joined within the period of limitation, the suit must be dismissed. The Division Bench further observed as follows: 

 "Section 22, the Limitation Act, provides, inter alia, that when a new party is added as plaintiff, the date of his being added is to be considered as regards him as the date of institution of the suit."

 12. In the instant case the agreement was entered into on 30-7-1979 and the suit was filed on 26-7-81. According to the plaint, plaintiffs request for execution and registration of the sale deed was refused by the defendant on 8-2-1981 and the plaintiff submitted as application before the trial Court on 31-1-1984 for making the government a defendant (Pro-defendant No. 2 in the suit). The order sheet of the trial Court shows that this application was filed on 31-1-1984 and was allowed by the Court on 29-3-84. So, it is clear that the application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed before the expiry of the period of limitation (3 years under Article 113 of the Limitation Act) on 7-2-84. It is therefore, clear that the suit for filing of the application under Order 1 rule 10 of the CPC cannot come within the mischief of limitation for failure of the trial Court to dispose of the matter in time. In this view of the matter, the trial Court rightly found that the suit was properly constituted and not barred by limitation.
